body_text: View All News Camden National Corporation Reports Record Quarterly Net Income of $23.0 Million and Diluted EPS of $1.35 for the Second Quarter of 2026 July 28, 2026 Record earnings reflect continued momentum and improved profitability CAMDEN, Maine , July 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Camden National Corporation (NASDAQ: CAC; "Camden National" or the "Company") reported net income of $23.0 million and diluted earnings per share ("EPS") of $1.35 for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, resulting in a return on average assets of 1.33%, a return on average equity of 12.92%, and a return on average tangible equity (non‑GAAP) of 18.47%. "Our record quarterly earnings reflect the momentum we are building across the franchise as we execute on our long-term strategy," said Simon Griffiths, President and Chief Executive Officer of Camden National Corporation. "Through continued investment in talent and focused efforts to deepen customer relationships, we delivered 3% annualized loan growth during the quarter and strong revenue performance across our complementary business lines. We enter the second half of the year with confidence in our strategy, disciplined execution, and a continued commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders." For the first six months of 2026, the Company reported record net income of $44.9 million and diluted EPS of $2.64, compared to $21.4 million and $1.26, respectively, for the six months ended June 30, 2025. Results benefited from the successful integration and earnings contribution of Northway Financial, Inc., acquired on January 1, 2025, as well as continued growth in core business activities. On a non-GAAP basis, adjusted pre-tax, pre-provision income increased 19% to $58.7 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026. SECOND QUARTER 2026 HIGHLIGHTS Net income and diluted EPS for the second quarter of 2026 each increased 5% over the first quarter of 2026. Total revenue for the second quarter of 2026 increased 5% over the first quarter of 2026, driven by net interest margin expansion of 2 basis points to 3.26% and strong non-interest income growth of 21%. The GAAP efficiency ratio for the second quarter was 55.42%, and the non-GAAP efficiency ratio was 53.23%, compared to 55.50% and 53.21%, respectively, for the first quarter of 2026. Loans grew 1% during the second quarter of 2026, and the committed loan pipeline increased 45% from the first quarter of 2026. Book value per share increased to $42.96 and tangible book value per share (non-GAAP) increased to $31.64 at June 30, 2026, from $41.98 and $30.58, respectively, at March 31, 2026. The Company repurchased 52,000 shares of its common stock at a weighted-average price of $47.64 per share during the second quarter of 2026. FINANCIAL OPERATING RESULTS (Q2 2026 vs. Q1 2026) Net interest income for the second quarter of 2026 totaled $52.9 million, an increase of 1% from the first quarter of 2026. Net interest margin expanded 2 basis points on a linked-quarter basis to 3.26% for the second quarter of 2026, driven by lower funding costs. On a non-GAAP basis, core net interest margin increased 5 basis points over the same period to 2.97% for the second quarter of 2026. For the second quarter of 2026, net fair value mark accretion income of $4.0 million was recognized, a decrease of $335,000 from the first quarter of 2026. Provision expense was $710,000 for the second quarter of 2026, compared to $553,000 for the first quarter of 2026. During the second quarter of 2026, loans grew 1% while asset quality remained strong, as evidenced by an annualized net charge-offs-to-average-loans ratio of 0.04% for the quarter. Non-interest income for the second quarter of 2026 totaled $14.5 million, an increase of $2.5 million, or 21% compared to the first quarter of 2026. Quarter-over-quarter, revenue across all non-interest income categories increased, including deposit customer-related revenue, debit card income, and our wealth and brokerage businesses. As of June 30, 2026, assets under administration across our wealth and brokerage businesses totaled $2.6 billion, an increase of 13% over the same period a year ago. Non-interest expense for the second quarter of 2026 totaled $37.4 million, a 5% increase compared to the first quarter of 2026. The increase was primarily driven by annual salary increases and the timing of our annual director equity award grant and recognition event for our top-performing sales team members, both of which occur in the second quarter each year. The Company's GAAP and non‑GAAP efficiency ratios for the second quarter of 2026 were 55.42% and 53.23% compared to 55.50% and 53.21%, respectively, for the first quarter of 2026. FINANCIAL CONDITION Total assets were $7.0 billion at both June 30, 2026 and March 31, 2026. Investments totaled $1.4 billion at June 30, 2026, representing a 1% decrease from March 31, 2026. Total loans were $5.0 billion as of June 30, 2026, an increase of 1% from March 31, 2026, driven by increases in our home equity and commercial loan portfolios of 7% and 4%, respectively, during the quarter. The Company ended the second quarter with a committed loan pipeline of $185.7 million, up 45% from the prior quarter. The Company's asset quality remained strong during the quarter, with past-due loans representing 0.15% and non-performing loans 0.24% of total loans at June 30, 2026. The allowance for credit losses ("ACL") on loans was 0.91% of total loans, compared with 0.92% at March 31, 2026. The ACL coverage ratio was 3.8 times non-performing loans as of June 30, 2026, compared to 4.2 times as of March 31, 2026. Deposits totaled $5.6 billion at June 30, 2026, representing a 1% decrease from March 31, 2026, driven by lower brokered deposits and certificates of deposit as the Company continued to optimize its funding mix. Core deposits remained stable during the quarter, supported by continued growth in the Company's high-yield savings product and the durability of its customer deposit base. As of June 30, 2026, the Company's loan-to-deposit ratio was 90%, compared with 89% at March 31, 2026. As of June 30, 2026, the Company maintained capital ratios well in excess of all regulatory requirements, including a Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of 12.19%, a Tier 1 risk-based ratio of 13.48%, a total risk-based ratio of 14.43%, and a Tier 1 leverage ratio of 9.66%. For the first six months of 2026, the Company repurchased 85,131 shares at a weighted average price of $46.55 per share under its share repurchase program. The Company announced a cash dividend of $0.42 per share, representing an annualized dividend yield of 3.10%, based on the Company's closing share price of $54.22 as reported by NASDAQ on June 30, 2026. The dividend will be payable on July 31, 2026, to shareholders of record on July 15, 2026. Q2 2026 CONFERENCE CALL Camden National Corporation will host a conference call and webcast at 3:00 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, to discuss its second quarter of 2026 financial results and outlook. Participants should dial into the call 10 - 15 minutes before it begins. Information about the conference call is as follows: Live dial-in (Domestic): (833) 461-5787 Link to obtain live dial-in (All other locations): https://help.events.q4inc.com/eahc/international-dial-in-numbers Meeting ID: 727 027 679 Live webcast URL: https://events.q4inc.com/attendee/727027679 A link to the live webcast will be available on Camden National's website under "Resources — Investor Relations" at CamdenNational.bank before the meeting, and a replay of the webcast will be available on Camden National's website following the conference call. The conference call transcript will also be available on Camden National's website approximately two days after the conference call. ABOUT CAMDEN NATIONAL CORPORATION Camden National Corporation (NASDAQ: CAC) is Northern New England's largest publicly traded bank holding company, with $7.0 billion in assets. Founded in 1875, Camden National Bank has 72 banking centers in Maine and New Hampshire and is a full-service community bank offering the latest digital banking, complemented by award-winning, personalized service. Additional information is available at CamdenNational.bank . Member FDIC. Equal Housing Lender. title: The Quoting Guide: Why Sales Teams Lose Quotes (and How to Prevent It)
summary: Quoting is where deals are won or lost. In industries like fasteners, valves, and industrial distribution, speed and consistency matter more than anything else.
body_text: The Quoting Guide covers the four biggest reasons sales teams lose quotes, backed by research and what you can do about it. 1. Quotes take too long to send The longer it takes to get a quote out, the more likely you are to lose the deal. Speed decides RFQ outcomes: Research consistently shows that faster responses dramatically increase conversion. InsideSales data shows that waiting more than 5 minutes can drop conversion rates by 8×. Tip: Set up a process where reps can build and send a quote in minutes. Speed is everything. 2. Follow-ups are inconsistent Sending a quote isn’t enough. Without reminders or structure, many quotes are never followed up on. Research on inside sales shows that consistent follow-up intensity leads to higher win rates. Manual follow-ups almost always slip through the cracks. Tip: Use a system that automatically flags open quotes and sets reminders for reps. Treat every quote like a lead that needs nurturing . 3. No data on quote-to-win ratio If you don’t know how many quotes are converting, you can’t improve. Most teams guess their close rate instead of tracking it. Tip: Start measuring. Track how many quotes go out, how many convert, and where the drop-offs happen (price, response time, lack of follow-up). Data should drive decisions. 4. Too much admin, not enough selling Sales reps are hired to build relationships. Instead, they spend hours on copy-paste work: retyping part numbers, digging through email chains, and updating spreadsheets. Studies on lead management show that without structure, reps get stuck in reactive work instead of selling. Tip: Eliminate repetitive admin wherever possible. Standardize templates, automate logging, and free up reps to focus on customers. Sources Oldroyd, J., & McElheran, K. (Harvard Business Review). The Short Life of Online Sales Leads — average response time 42 hours, 7× more likely to qualify within 1 hour. HBR Link InsideSales.com (now XANT). title: Higher education analytics for the ultra-intelligent university
summary: Learn how higher education analytics and a unified data platform help institutions break down silos and build a smarter, AI-ready university....
body_text: Higher education analytics for the ultra-intelligent university By Oksana Abramovych July 21, 2026 Share on Twitter Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook Share on Facebook Share by Email Share by Email Print this page Print The rise of the intelligent institution For modern universities, a seamless digital experience is an essential component to providing the resources and services that make an institution run. Following a rapid acceleration in digital transformation in recent years, students, staff, and partners now expect always-on services, consistent online experiences, and secure access to digital tools as a baseline. For universities, “ultra-intelligence” is an operational necessity. But most institutions aren’t there yet. As colleges evolve, one thing is clear: Universities need to move from task-specific work and department-only strategy and take a bigger-picture, institution-wide approach to technology. While many schools and universities are focused on higher education analytics and the promise of AI, they’re missing a key component to creating an ultra-intelligent institution: connected data. Data silos in higher education institutions Higher education institutions are often faced with silos as far as the eye can see: siloed tech tools, siloed teams, siloed budgets, and siloed resources spread across buildings, departments, and campuses. Universities often lack a common data repository from which to draw insights. Adopting a holistic approach to IT is a significant shift for most institutions, providing a unified point of visibility for aggregated analysis of all IT hardware, apps, and infrastructure. With a fragmented data environment, institutions lack real-time visibility into big-picture issues. Multiple data systems across different departments and programs lead to unnecessary exposure to security threats and a lack of overall institutional governance around data handling. To help break down these silos, a unified data platform can consolidate tech tools to reduce data sprawl, facilitate better collaboration, and become a truly data-driven institution. It’s easier said than done, however, especially when dealing with legacy apps and a culture that’s tied to existing technology and processes. The efficacy of an ultra-intelligent institution depends on the data that flows through it, where data is stored, and the ability to correlate data from multiple sources. With siloed data layered across teams and departments, teams struggle with a lack of real-time visibility. How can you make decisions based on data if you can’t see it all at once? Higher education analytics starts with connected data By rallying both institutional strategy and the IT services team around a unified data platform across academic, operational, and security systems, universities can aggregate, access, find, and act on all of their data from one source. Taking this approach can provide real-time access to critical information and the context to analyze that data and act on it quickly . When thinking about how to break down silos and build a unified platform, one successful strategy is to start with consolidating institutional data on IT infrastructure and then expanding into adjacent use cases. These datasets typically have the fewest privacy- and policy-related concerns for consolidation and offer significant operational and financial ROI. Elastic’s search-based platform helps ultra-intelligent institutions unify structured, unstructured, and semi-structured data from across their organization. With that data foundation in place, institutions can make faster, more informed decisions across critical areas — from application performance monitoring (APM) and threat hunting to protecting researchers’ intellectual property and keeping digital course catalogs and learning management systems reliable during enrollment surges. From data visibility to higher education innovation Building a holistic approach to IT in higher education requires a unified view into the entire IT environment. An end-to-end observability solution consolidates metrics, logs, and traces, so IT teams can see across them all, plus get the intelligence to detect anomalies, find patterns, and reduce mean time to resolution. With real-time visibility into your entire network, you can turn your institutional data into action and have an immediate impact on: Student services: As teams look to improve the student experience, holistic data insights can play a key role. Having the ability to quickly identify and predict issues can be instrumental in ensuring students can find the information they need, stay productive, and connect to the online tools and services that are essential to their day-to-day learning. IT operations: With IT operations consolidated, you’ll have the ability to implement efficient, streamlined processes across departments and the flexibility to spread resources as needed. With agile IT operations, you can look forward and take steps to implement new technologies as they come to market. Cybersecurity : As long as there are disconnected tools, systems, and data in your IT environment, there will be potential for gaps and hiding places where intrusions and malware can go undetected for months or even years. With a streamlined data strategy, your institution will be exposed to fewer vendors and vulnerabilities. And when faced with security threats, you’ll be able to act quickly and decisively, knowing what systems are compromised and require attention. What intelligent institutions look like in practice When an institution implements a unified data platform, it frees up countless hours for staff to experiment and innovate. Elastic’s agile platforms helped staff at these institutions create forward-looking solutions to complex technical problems. Georgia State University increases data insights with AI-powered search Georgia State University switched from native observability tools and streamlined its operations with a unified system built using Elasticsearch and Kibana dashboards on AWS. With that change, the IT team had time to experiment with new technologies and build a proof-of-concept AI-powered application to help students navigate the financial aid process. The tool assists students with personalized information and advice that helps guide them through the complicated and often confusing steps necessary to complete aid applications. Texas A&M University System saves over 100 analyst hours per month with AI The Texas A&M University System ’s cybersecurity operations team is tasked with protecting the data of 11 campuses, eight state agencies, and the second-largest student body in the US. They switched from using multiple security products to employing Elastic Security automatically on all devices, reducing the volume of documentation during security workflows, duplicate detections, and false positives. The switch saved the team more than 100 work hours per month, lowered incident resolution time, and enabled the rapid integration of additional security features and updates. The Maryland Innovation and Security Institute (MISI) operates a cost-effective security operations center The Maryland Innovation and Security Institute (MISI) is a nonprofit organization that trains young cyber professionals and helps institutions better understand the technology they’re evaluating so they can make informed decisions prior to investment. MISI uses Elastic Observability and Elastic Security as well as the AWS GovCloud FedRAMP Moderate authorized Elastic Cloud offering on many of its projects, including helping cyber defenders build their security skills in real-world environments. Building the foundation for higher education innovation and AI A streamlined, efficient data strategy is the first step to building an ultra-intelligent institution. It is the foundation that enables innovation and lays the groundwork for AI-powered solutions. AI holds promise and possibilities for higher education institutions, but in order to implement effective AI-powered tools, institutions must have a few key elements in place. An effective AI strategy requires: Access to trusted data: AI-powered solutions are only as strong as the data they’re built on. Without a solid foundation created from your institution’s proprietary data, your AI strategy will go nowhere. Strong institutional governance: If you plan to integrate AI into your IT toolkit, it’s essential that your institution implements an AI governance framework that outlines the rules and regulations around the creation and use of artificial intelligence across the university. Accessibility: In order for an institution to implement effective AI-powered solutions, you’ll need a unified platform that is widely available and easy for key stakeholders to access and use. Intelligence is built, not bought When it comes to building an ultra-intelligent university, one thing is for certain: There is no one quick fix. Intelligence at scale can’t be bought with a single product or tool. Instead, universities cultivate an environment of intelligence when they build and maintain streamlined, system-level capabilities across programs and departments. Connected, secure, real-time systems enable transparency and transformation. The good news is that a unified data platform can solve multiple problems simultaneously. Not only can it improve the uptime and usability of IT systems, but ultra-intelligent institutions will also be able to leverage their unified data platform’s speed — coupled with AI/ML capabilities — to quickly detect and respond to cyber threats before they compromise valuable data and pose a threat to institutional infrastructure. title: 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan Pricing, Specs, and Release Date
summary: Volkswagen's best-selling model, the Tiguan compact crossover SUV, was redesigned last year and returns for 2026 with a new, more powerful top-of-the-line trim.
body_text: The Volkswagen Tiguan sits between the subcompact Taos and the large Atlas SUVs in the German automaker’s lineup. The 2026 Tiguan competes against strong-selling crossover SUVs such as the Ford Bronco Sport, the Honda CR-V, the Hyundai Tucson, the Kia Sportage, the Mazda CX-50 and CX-5, the Nissan Rogue, the Subaru Forester, and the Toyota RAV4. With such formidable competition for buyers in the most popular vehicle segment in the United States, Volkswagen’s efforts to keep the Tiguan fresh have paid dividends and made it the brand’s best-selling nameplate in the U.S. and globally. 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan Pricing, Specs, and Release Date What’s New for the 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan Design Powertrain Interior Technology Safety Pricing and Release Date Further Research What’s New for the 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan Volkswagen rolled out an all-new Tiguan in 2025, and while nothing has changed on the outside this year, the manufacturer expanded the model range for 2026 with the addition of a top-of-the-line SEL R-Line Turbo trim level. This new variant benefits from a more powerful turbocharged four-cylinder engine, standard all-wheel drive (AWD), and more standard features than any other Tiguan model. Design The Tiguan lost its optional third row when it was redesigned in 2025 (which was too small to be particularly useful anyway), and some heft, but its exterior dimensions actually grew a little. From the outside, the 2026 Tiguan looks classy with sculpted flanks, arched rear haunches, and a broad grille. In S and SE trim levels, the 2026 VW Tiguan looks comparatively plain, but the SE R-Line Black and new-for-2026 SEL R-Line Turbo amp up the looks with fancier wheels and a front fascia that adds sporty air intakes on either side of the blacked-out grille. Powertrain The 2026 VW Tiguan comes standard with a turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine that produces 201 horsepower and 207 pound-feet of torque. Front-wheel drive (FWD) is standard, and AWD is available. The SEL R-Line Turbo gains a more powerful engine, though displacement remains the same. With 268 hp and standard AWD, the top-of-the-line Tiguan should be much quicker around town than less-expensive models. An eight-speed automatic transmission is used in all Tiguans. With its base engine and FWD, the 2026 Tiguan is estimated to return 26 mpg in the city, 30 mpg on the highway, and 29 mpg combined. Adding AWD drops those figures to 22/32/25 mpg. With its more powerful engine, the Tiguan SEL R-Line Turbo’s figures sit at 25/32/28 mpg with FWD or 22/29/25 mpg with AWD. Properly equipped, the 2026 Tiguan can tow up to 1,800 pounds, which is well below segment leaders that can tow up to 3,500 pounds. Interior The Tiguan’s interior is modern and classy, with smart, quality materials. The Tiguan S model wears cloth upholstery with interesting patterns on the seats and door panels. The SE model offers three different leatherette color options and a 10-color ambient lighting package. The SE R-Line Black has its own unique interior trim and a leather-wrapped steering wheel, while the top SEL R-Line Turbo gets perforated leather upholstery in three hues and 30-color ambient lighting. The 2026 Tiguan offers 37.6 cubic feet of cargo capacity with the rear seats in place or 73.4 when they're folded down. That’s behind the Hyundai Tucson (up to 80.3 cubic feet), the Honda CR-V (76.5 cubic feet), and the Kia Sportage (up to 74.1 cubic feet), but still above average for the segment. Technology A 12.9-inch infotainment screen comes standard in the 2026 Tiguan S, SE, and SE R-Line Black, while the Tiguan SEL R-Line Turbo gets an exclusive 15-inch touchscreen. Both touchscreen infotainment systems use the same Digital Cockpit Pro software, and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard across the lineup. Thankfully, a physical knob for audio control is also included. A 10.25-inch Digital Cockpit Pro digital gauge cluster is standard on all 2026 Tiguan models. In addition, the SE R-Line Black and SEL R-Line Turbo come standard with a head-up display that projects information on the windshield in front of the driver. A seven-speaker audio system is standard, and SEL R-Line Turbo models get a 700-watt Harman Kardon system with 12 speakers. Travel Assist (semi-automated hands-on driving assistance with assisted lane changing), forward-collision warning, automatic emergency braking with pedestrian monitoring, rear-traffic alert, stop-and-go adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, and emergency assist (semi-automated vehicle assistance in a medical emergency) are all standard. The 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan has been tested by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) and received a Good rating in the small overlap front crash test and updated side test, but earned a Poor rating in the updated moderate overlap front crashworthiness test. The Tiguan received the maximum five-star overall safety rating from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). Pricing and Release Date At the time of writing, the 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan started at $32,280 in base S trim with FWD, including a $1,475 destination charge. Opting for AWD raises the base price to $33,780. The SE trim starts at $35,080 or $36,580 with AWD, and a panoramic sunroof is optional for an extra $1,200. In SE R-Line Black trim, the 2026 Tiguan carries an MSRP of $38,720 or $40,220 with AWD. The top SEL R-Line Turbo model starts at $44,560 and comes standard with AWD.
